questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: A 15 kg child is given rapid crystalloid and SBP remains ≤ 80 mmHg. After what crystalloid volume should blood products be considered?
questions.explanation: The pediatric trigger is 20 mL/kg of crystalloid with SBP still ≤ 80 mmHg (20 × 15 kg = 300 mL); 500 mL is the adult trigger and 10 mL/kg is the pediatric blood product volume.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: After an IV fluid bolus, what shock index (HR/SBP) triggers blood products in a child aged 7 – 12?
questions.explanation: Shock index thresholds rise as age falls because normal heart rates are higher: > 0.9 at age ≥ 13, > 1.0 at 7 – 12 and > 1.22 at 4 – 6.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: A 5-year-old has HR 150 and SBP 120 after an IV fluid bolus. What is the shock index, and does it meet the blood product trigger for that age?
questions.explanation: Shock index is HR/SBP = 150/120 = 1.25, which exceeds the > 1.22 threshold for age 4 – 6, so blood products should be considered. 0.8 is the inverted SBP/HR mistake.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: In obvious class III or IV hemorrhagic shock, what is infused in place of crystalloid boluses when it is available?
questions.explanation: Crystalloid dilutes clotting factors in hemorrhage; the guideline directs plasma, when available, in lieu of crystalloid boluses for obvious class III/IV shock.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: An adult in hemorrhagic shock meets criteria for blood products but no LTOWB is carried. What is given?
options: Plasma and PRBC together on one IV set
questions.explanation: LTOWB 1 unit is first-line; if it is not available, proceed to component therapy — plasma 1 unit then PRBC 1 unit, each if available. Plasma and RBCs may not run simultaneously through the same set.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: A patient develops transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) during a transfusion. Beyond stopping the transfusion, what will likely be required?
questions.explanation: TRALI is non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema; oxygen to SpO2 > 93% is the first step but intubation and PPV will likely be required. Anaphylaxis and urticaria are treated via the anaphylaxis guideline.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: What is done with the blood units suspected of causing a transfusion reaction?
options: Deliver them to the receiving facility
Discard them in a biohazard bag
Return them to the aircraft blood cooler
Restart them at a slower rate
questions.explanation: Implicated units are evidence for the reaction work-up: keep them, deliver them to the receiving facility and notify the sending blood bank as required.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: A child develops fever during a transfusion. What acetaminophen dose is given?
questions.explanation: Pediatric transfusion fever gets acetaminophen 15 mg/kg IV over 15 minutes with a 750 mg maximum; 1 gram is the pediatric TXA ceiling and 50 mg/kg is the calcium gluconate dose.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: O-negative RBCs are not available. Which patient may receive O-positive RBCs or LTOWB without the extra notification required for at-risk patients?
questions.explanation: O-positive product is acceptable for all males, women s/p hysterectomy or beyond child-bearing age (usually ≥ 50) and females with documented Rh-positive type; females < 50 risk Rh sensitization.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: In imminent risk of death, O-positive LTOWB is given to a 28-year-old female of unknown Rh type. Who must be notified?
options: Sending physician and sending blood bank
CMOC only, at the end of the shift
Receiving physician, CMOC and LFN Medical Director
questions.explanation: O-positive product to a female < 50 not known to be Rh positive requires notifying the receiving physician, the Clinical Manager On Call and the LFN Medical Director, plus a QM report for tracking.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: How may plasma and RBCs be given through the same IV set?
options: They may never share an IV set
questions.explanation: Plasma and RBCs may share a set if run one after the other; if multiple lines are available they may be given simultaneously on separate lines.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: A patient needs a transfusion rate faster than the blood warming device can provide. What is directed?
options: Never exceed the warmer's maximum rate
Bridge with crystalloid until blood is warmed
Weigh rapid transfusion against giving cold blood
Stop and wait for warmed product
questions.explanation: A warmer is used when possible, but if the required rate exceeds it the crew weighs the benefit of rapid transfusion against the risk of cold blood rather than delaying resuscitation.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: When is temperature checked to detect a transfusion reaction?
options: Before, and 5 min after starting each unit
Before, and 15 min after starting each unit
Only before the first unit is started
questions.explanation: Take a pre-transfusion temperature and recheck 15 minutes after initiation, repeating for every unit; fever (T > 38°C or a 1°C rise) suggests a reaction.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: A patient arrives with a TXA infusion started before your arrival. What is done with it?
options: Stop it and give a 2 gram bolus
Stop it, TXA is given only as a bolus
Stop it until blood products finish
questions.explanation: A pre-existing TXA infusion is continued (generally run over 8 hours). LFN gives its own TXA as a one-time bolus, which is why the receiving team is told no infusion was started.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: What SBP target applies to a 6-year-old receiving blood products who has a suspected head injury?
questions.explanation: With head injury the pediatric target is 90 + (age × 2) = 90 + 12 = 102 mmHg; 80 mmHg is the target without head injury and 110 mmHg is the adult head-injury target.

questions.title: Blood Product Administration
questions.stem: What tranexamic acid dose is given to a 24 kg child receiving blood products within 2 hours of injury?
questions.explanation: Pediatric TXA is 15 mg/kg IV over 10 minutes mixed in 100 mL NS (15 × 24 = 360 mg), well under the 1 gram maximum; 1,200 mg is the calcium gluconate 50 mg/kg error.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: A hypotensive patient with suspected cardiac ischemia needs rapid vasopressor support before an infusion. Which push dose agent is preferred?
questions.explanation: Epinephrine is preferred only when the patient is bradycardic with no suspected cardiac ischemia; norepinephrine is preferred for all other patients.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: Which epinephrine concentration is drawn from to prepare push dose epinephrine?
questions.explanation: Push dose epinephrine starts from the 0.1 mg/mL product; 1 mL added to 9 mL of saline yields 10 mcg/mL. Using 1 mg/mL would make a tenfold overdose syringe.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: After 1 mL of 0.1 mg/mL epinephrine is added to the prepared saline flush, how much epinephrine does the push dose syringe contain in total?
questions.explanation: 1 mL × 0.1 mg/mL = 0.1 mg = 100 mcg, spread through 10 mL to give 10 mcg/mL. 10 mcg is the per-mL concentration, not the syringe total.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: An ordered push dose of 20 mcg epinephrine is drawn from the 10 mcg/mL syringe. What volume is pushed?
questions.explanation: Volume = dose ÷ concentration = 20 mcg ÷ 10 mcg/mL = 2 mL. The whole 10 mL syringe holds only 100 mcg.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: Push dose norepinephrine is mixed at 16 mcg/mL and 10 mL is drawn into a syringe. How much norepinephrine is in that syringe?
questions.explanation: 16 mcg/mL × 10 mL = 160 mcg. The mix is 4 mg (4 mL of 1 mg/mL) in a 250 mL NS bag; 100 mcg is the epinephrine syringe total.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: What is the first step when preparing and giving push dose epinephrine?
options: Remove 1 mL of saline from the flush
Connect flush and amp to a 3-way stopcock
Add 1 mL of epinephrine to the flush
questions.explanation: Patency is confirmed first so a vasopressor is not extravasated; then 1 mL is removed from the 10 mL flush, the flush and amp are joined at a stopcock, and 1 mL of epinephrine is added.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: After 10 mL of the push dose norepinephrine mixture is drawn into a syringe, what is done with the 250 mL bag?
options: Spike it with pump tubing and start the infusion ASAP
Discard it once the syringe is labeled
Hold it unspiked unless pushes fail
Dilute it further for pediatric use
questions.explanation: Push doses are a bridge: the same 16 mcg/mL bag becomes the infusion, so it is labeled, spiked with pump tubing and started as soon as possible.

questions.title: Push Dose Vasopressors
questions.stem: An adult trauma patient has HR 104 and SBP 128. What is the shock index, and what does it suggest?
questions.explanation: SI = HR/SBP = 104/128 = 0.81. An SI ≥ 0.8 is highly sensitive for occult shock even with a normal-looking SBP, and can guide fluids and push dose pressors.
